title: Trigonometry
lines: Trigonometry questions reward memory: if you know the special values, the identities and the shape of y = A sin(ωx + φ), most items take under a minute.
## Radians and arc length
- Arc length l = rθ and sector area S = ½r²θ = ½lr (θ in radians).
> Example: A sector has radius 4 and central angle 3π/4. Find its arc length and area.
! Trap: arc and sector formulas only work with θ in radians. Convert degrees first.
## Unit-circle definitions and signs
- For the point P(x, y) where the terminal side of angle α meets the unit circle: sin α = y, cos α = x, tan α = y/x (x ≠ 0).
- For any point (x, y) on the terminal side at distance r = √(x² + y²): sin α = y/r, cos α = x/r, tan α = y/x.
- Signs: Quadrant I all positive; II sin positive; III tan positive; IV cos positive.
> Example: The terminal side of α passes through (−3, 4). Find sin α and cos α.
## Special angle values
- cos runs the same list backwards: cos 0 = 1, cos π/6 = √3/2, cos π/4 = √2/2, cos π/3 = 1/2, cos π/2 = 0.
- tan π/6 = √3/3, tan π/4 = 1, tan π/3 = √3; tan π/2 is undefined.
## Basic identities
- sin²α + cos²α = 1 and tan α = sin α / cos α.
- 1 + tan²α = 1/cos²α.
> Example: sin α = 3/5 and α is in Quadrant II. Find cos α and tan α.
> cos²α = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25. In Quadrant II cos is negative: cos α = −4/5. tan α = −3/4.
> Example: tan α = 2. Find (sin α + cos α)/(sin α − cos α).
> Divide top and bottom by cos α: (tan α + 1)/(tan α − 1) = 3/1 = 3.
! Trick: for expressions homogeneous in sin and cos, divide by cos α (or by cos²α, using sin²α + cos²α as the denominator for things like sin α cos α).
> Example: tan α = 2. Find sin α cos α.
> sin α cos α / (sin²α + cos²α) = tan α / (tan²α + 1) = 2/5.
## Reduction (induction) formulas
- For angles kπ ± α: the function name stays the same. For π/2 ± α or 3π/2 ± α: sin and cos swap.
- The sign is the sign of the original function in the quadrant where the angle would lie if α were acute.
- Key ones: sin(π − α) = sin α, cos(π − α) = −cos α, sin(π + α) = −sin α, cos(π + α) = −cos α, sin(−α) = −sin α, cos(−α) = cos α, sin(π/2 − α) = cos α, cos(π/2 + α) = −sin α.
> Example: Evaluate sin(7π/6) and cos(−2π/3).
> Example: Evaluate tan(5π/4) + sin(13π/6).
> tan(π + π/4) = tan π/4 = 1. sin(13π/6) = sin(2π + π/6) = 1/2. Total 3/2.
## Sum, difference and double angle
- sin(α ± β) = sin α cos β ± cos α sin β.
- cos(α ± β) = cos α cos β ∓ sin α sin β (note the opposite sign).
- tan(α ± β) = (tan α ± tan β)/(1 ∓ tan α tan β).
- sin 2α = 2 sin α cos α.
- cos 2α = cos²α − sin²α = 2cos²α − 1 = 1 − 2sin²α.
- tan 2α = 2 tan α / (1 − tan²α).
- Power reduction: cos²α = (1 + cos 2α)/2, sin²α = (1 − cos 2α)/2.
- Auxiliary angle: a sin x + b cos x = √(a² + b²) sin(x + φ), where tan φ = b/a; the maximum is √(a² + b²).
> Example: Evaluate sin 75°.
> Example: Evaluate cos 15° cos 45° + sin 15° sin 45°.
> Example: tan α = 1/2, tan β = 1/3, both acute. Find α + β.
> Example: sin α = 1/3. Find cos 2α.
> Example: Maximum of y = sin x + √3 cos x.
> √(1 + 3) = 2, so y = 2 sin(x + π/3) and the maximum is 2.
! Trap: sin 2α is not 2 sin α. And when a question gives sin α only, the sign of cos α depends on the quadrant; read the range of α.
## Graphs of sin, cos and tan
- y = sin x: period 2π, range [−1, 1], odd, maxima at x = π/2 + 2kπ.
- y = cos x: period 2π, range [−1, 1], even, maxima at x = 2kπ.
- y = tan x: period π, range R, odd, undefined at x = π/2 + kπ, increasing on each interval (−π/2 + kπ, π/2 + kπ).
- sin x increases on [−π/2 + 2kπ, π/2 + 2kπ]; cos x decreases on [2kπ, π + 2kπ].
## y = A sin(ωx + φ) + B
- Amplitude |A|; period T = 2π/|ω|; phase shift −φ/ω; vertical shift B; maximum B + |A|, minimum B − |A|.
- For y = A tan(ωx + φ) the period is π/|ω|.
- Symmetry axes are where ωx + φ = π/2 + kπ; symmetry centres are where ωx + φ = kπ.
- To get y = sin(2x + π/3) from y = sin 2x, shift left by π/6 (not π/3), because sin(2x + π/3) = sin 2(x + π/6).
> Example: y = 3 sin(2x − π/6) + 1. Find the period, the maximum and an x where it occurs.
> T = 2π/2 = π. Maximum 3 + 1 = 4 when 2x − π/6 = π/2, i.e. x = π/3.
> Example: Find an increasing interval of y = sin(2x + π/4).
> Example: The graph of y = 2 sin(ωx + φ) (ω > 0, |φ| < π/2) has neighbouring maximum and minimum at x = π/12 and x = 7π/12. Find ω and φ.
> Half a period is 7π/12 − π/12 = π/2, so T = π and ω = 2. At the maximum: 2 · π/12 + φ = π/2, so φ = π/3.
! Trap: when A or ω is negative, the increasing and decreasing intervals swap. Rewrite with positive ω first.
## Solving triangles
- Angle sum: A + B + C = π. Larger side faces larger angle.
- Sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R (R is the circumradius).
- Cosine rule: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, so cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc).
- Area S = ½ab sin C = ½bc sin A = ½ca sin B.
- Use the sine rule for two angles and a side, or two sides and an opposite angle; use the cosine rule for three sides or two sides and the included angle.
> Example: In triangle ABC, a = √3, b = 1, A = π/3. Find B.
> sin B = b sin A / a = (1 · √3/2)/√3 = 1/2. Since b < a, B < A, so B = π/6 (not 5π/6).
> Example: b = 3, c = 5, A = 2π/3. Find a and the area.
> Example: The sides are 3, 5, 7. Find the largest angle.
! Trap (ambiguous case): sin B = k has two solutions in (0, π), B and π − B. Keep π − B only if the angle sum stays below π and the larger side still faces the larger angle.
! Trick: if a question says a cos B = b cos A or similar, use the sine rule to turn sides into sines: sin A cos B − cos A sin B = 0 gives sin(A − B) = 0, so A = B (isosceles).
## Quick checklist
- Read the range of α before taking a square root.
- Convert degrees to radians when a formula needs it.
- For shifts, factor out ω: the shift is the amount added to x, not to ωx.
